subtype: Approach: designs a team project by listing how it would fall apart [Action]
passage: I'm Rajni, and I sat behind Lokesh's team in the design lab while they planned their final-year project. Instead of dividing up tasks, Lokesh asked the group, 'How could we make this project fall apart?' They wrote answers on the board: nobody knows who is doing what, everything gets merged the night before, and one of us can't be reached when needed. Then, quickly, they answered each one. A role for each person on a sheet. A merge every Friday, not at the end. And one page of everyone's contact numbers, two each. Lokesh photographed the board. I can't say whether they were excited or just efficient, but at the demo, when one member fell ill, someone else already knew that part.

qa.q: On which day of the week did the team plan to merge?
qa.a: They planned to merge every Friday.

qa.q: What might Lokesh have been feeling when asking how the project could fall apart?
qa.a: Lokesh was perhaps cautious and wanted to head off trouble, though Rajni can't be sure of the inner state.

qa.q: What other step could the team add to keep everyone in touch?
qa.a: The team could send a short message each evening saying what each person did, since it shows early when someone is stuck.

qa.q: How might the member who fell ill have felt when someone already knew that part?
qa.a: That member was probably relieved, since the work could go on without them.

grounding: Shows a student team listing how their project could fall apart and setting roles, weekly merges and a shared contact sheet.

subtype: Approach: only avoids bad outcomes and never defines a positive goal [Pitfall]
passage:
Monday: Raghav wrote his final-year plan as a list of things not to do: don't take a risky elective, don't join a busy club, don't apply anywhere he might not get in, don't pay for courses he might not finish. Preeti read it over his shoulder and said it looked safe.

Thursday: Raghav showed the plan to a senior and noticed that every line said what to avoid. No line said what he wanted. 'What are you aiming at?' asked Preeti. He couldn't say.

Following Monday: Raghav put down his pen. He had a plan that couldn't fail, and it also led nowhere. His week had been full of careful non-choices, and he still had no idea what he wanted to be doing in a year.

qa.q: What did every line of Raghav's plan say?
qa.a: Every line said what to avoid.

qa.q: How did Raghav feel when Preeti asked what he was aiming at?
qa.a: Raghav felt stuck and empty, since he couldn't answer and saw the plan pointed nowhere.

qa.q: What other step could Raghav take to build a real direction?
qa.a: Raghav could write down one thing he wants to be doing in a year and choose a small step toward it each month, keeping the avoid list as a side note.

qa.q: How might Preeti have seen the plan?
qa.a: Preeti probably saw a safe but empty plan, which is why Preeti said it looked safe and asked what Raghav was aiming at.

grounding: Shows a student who avoids every mistake he can think of, ending with a safe, empty plan and no positive goal.

subtype: Approach: asks how to make a situation worse to spot hidden levers [Thinking]
passage: Kashish, you say your meetings are chaos, so here's a trick from my own team. I'm Charu. Our meetings ran long and loud, and everyone complained but nobody knew where to start. So one Friday I asked the room, 'How would we make these meetings even worse?' People laughed, then answered fast: send the agenda five minutes before, and never write anything down, so we can argue later about what we agreed. Somebody said, 'We already do both.' That stopped us. We changed only those two things: agendas the evening before, and one person taking notes and sending them the same day. Within a month the meetings were forty minutes instead of an hour and a half, and the shouting faded. I still ask the 'worse' question when I'm stuck.

qa.q: How long were the meetings after a month?
qa.a: After a month the meetings were forty minutes.

qa.q: What was Charu feeling before asking the 'worse' question?
qa.a: Charu was stuck and probably frustrated, since everyone complained but nobody knew where to start.

qa.q: Which turning point made the hidden causes visible?
qa.a: Asking how to make the meetings worse and hearing 'We already do both' showed the causes, so two simple changes could be made.

qa.q: How might the team have felt when somebody said 'We already do both'?
qa.a: The team was probably struck by the truth in it, maybe a little embarrassed, since it stopped them.

grounding: Shows a manager asking what would make noisy meetings worse, spotting late agendas and no notes as hidden levers, and fixing those two.

subtype: Approach: pairs the list of things to avoid with a positive target [Revision]
passage: I'm Rehana, and I share a flat with Pallavi, so I watched her yearly plan take shape at the kitchen table. The first version was all rules: no takeaways, no late nights before work, no extra projects, no arguing with her manager. It looked tidy. On Sunday, though, she read it aloud, stopped, and said, 'This tells me what to avoid, not where I'm going.' She took a blank sheet, wrote the twelve months down the side, and beside each one put a single aim: finish the first module of her design course in February, present at the team demo in March, and so on. The rules went at the bottom of the page in small writing. I can't tell what she felt, but she pinned it above her desk and looked at it every morning.

qa.q: Where did Pallavi put the rules on the new sheet?
qa.a: Pallavi put the rules at the bottom of the page in small writing.

qa.q: What might Pallavi have been thinking when she stopped reading aloud?
qa.a: Pallavi may have realised that the plan was only about avoiding things and felt a little disappointed, though Rehana can't be sure.

qa.q: What could Pallavi do if she misses a monthly aim?
qa.a: Pallavi could move the aim to the next month and ask what got in the way, since the aims should guide the year and not become a source of guilt.

qa.q: How might Rehana have seen the change in the plan?
qa.a: Rehana probably noticed the plan going from tidy to purposeful, though Rehana can't say how Pallavi felt.

grounding: Shows a person noticing that a plan is only defensive and adding one clear aim per month, so avoidance rules serve a direction.

subtype: Approach: keeps asking why until a deeper cause appears [Thinking]
passage: Teacher's note. Kashish had lost her pencil box for the third time this term. This time I asked her not to look for it first, but to ask 'why' out loud. 'Why do I lose it?' 'I leave it at school.' 'Why do I leave it?' 'I rush at the bell.' 'Why do I rush?' Kashish thought for a while. 'Because I only start packing when the bell rings, and Chinmay is already waiting at the door.' She grinned. 'So I should pack before the bell.' The next day Kashish began packing five minutes early. By Friday the box came home every day.

qa.q: How many times had Kashish lost the pencil box this term?
qa.a: Kashish had lost the pencil box for the third time this term.

qa.q: What did Kashish's grin suggest?
qa.a: Kashish's grin suggested she was pleased, since she had found the cause and a plan of her own.

qa.q: What other step could help Kashish remember the box?
qa.a: Kashish could keep a small picture card in her bag listing what to pack, since a card reminds her even on rushed days.

qa.q: How might Chinmay have seen Kashish packing early?
qa.a: Chinmay was probably glad to leave without waiting at the door, since Kashish was ready when the bell rang.

grounding: Shows a girl who keeps losing her pencil box asking why again and again until she finds the deeper cause and packs before the bell.

subtype: Approach: traces a repeated problem to its underlying cause [Thinking]
passage: Tuesday. Got 9 out of 25 in the maths test again. Sat with the paper and asked myself why instead of just feeling rubbish. Why did I lose marks? Mostly careless errors: wrong signs, copied numbers. Why careless? I was rushing. Why rushing? I ran out of time on the last section. Why did I run out? The early questions took me ages. Why so slow on those? I haven't practised the early chapters for months; I jumped ahead. So it isn't that I'm bad at maths. It's that the easy topics are slow. Told Pradeep Sir, and he said to try ten minutes of quick early-chapter sums every day. I'll test that for two weeks. — Hrithik

qa.q: What was Hrithik's score in the test?
qa.a: Hrithik got 9 out of 25.

qa.q: How does Hrithik feel after asking why so many times?
qa.a: Hrithik feels less rubbish and more hopeful, since the trouble is slow early topics and not being bad at maths.

qa.q: What other step could Hrithik use to check the plan is working?
qa.a: Hrithik could time each section in practice tests, since it shows whether the early questions are getting faster.

qa.q: How might Pradeep Sir have seen Hrithik's explanation?
qa.a: Pradeep Sir was probably pleased that Hrithik had traced the reasons alone, which made a clear daily practice easy to suggest.

grounding: Shows a student failing maths tests asking why repeatedly and tracing it from careless errors to rushing, to slow early questions, to too little practice of early topics.

subtype: Approach: acts on the root cause found rather than the symptom [Action]
passage: Nilesh had been late to the eight o'clock lecture nine times in a month, and Binita, the hostel warden, asked him to stop by her office. Instead of scolding, she asked, 'Why are you late?' 'I wake up late.' 'Why?' 'I sleep late.' 'Why?' He shrugged. 'I scroll on my phone in bed until two.' 'And why do you scroll?' 'I just keep doing it. It's a habit.' Nilesh looked at the floor. He didn't need a louder alarm; he needed the phone out of reach. That night he put the charger on a shelf in the corridor, beyond the reach of his bed. By Friday he was in his seat at ten to eight.

qa.q: How many times was Nilesh late in a month?
qa.a: Nilesh was late nine times in a month.

qa.q: Why might Nilesh have looked at the floor?
qa.a: Nilesh probably felt embarrassed and a little uncomfortable admitting that scrolling was a habit he couldn't stop.

qa.q: What other step could help Nilesh keep to the change?
qa.a: Nilesh could ask a roommate to check that the phone is charging in the corridor at night, since a small promise to someone else helps a new habit last.

qa.q: How might Binita have seen Nilesh's answers?
qa.a: Binita was probably concerned but patient, since she asked why step by step and did not scold.

grounding: Shows a hostel student tracing lateness to poor sleep, then late phone use, then a scrolling habit, and acting on that cause by charging the phone away from the bed.

subtype: Approach: stops at a convenient answer and blames a person [Pitfall]
passage: I'm Ramesh, and I'll tell you about the outage I'm least proud of. A config change took our site down for an hour. In the meeting I asked once, 'Why did it go down?' and the answer was, 'Kamal pushed a wrong value.' Everyone nodded, relieved to have an answer. I told Kamal to be more careful, and we moved on. Kamal was quiet for a week. Then, six weeks later, someone else pushed a wrong value and the site went down again. That's when it hit me: I had never asked why a wrong value could reach the live site at all. No test caught it, and nobody was clearly in charge of reviewing config. Kamal wasn't the cause. Kamal was just the person nearest the button.

qa.q: How long after the first outage did the second one happen?
qa.a: The second outage happened six weeks later.

qa.q: How might Kamal have felt after being told to be more careful?
qa.a: Kamal probably felt ashamed and unfairly singled out, shown by being quiet for a week.

qa.q: What other approach could Ramesh have used in the first meeting?
qa.a: Ramesh could have kept asking why until a process cause appeared, such as why no test caught the wrong value and who reviews config.

qa.q: How might Kamal's teammates have felt at the first meeting?
qa.a: They were probably relieved at first to have a simple answer, though the second outage would leave them uneasy.

grounding: Shows a team asking why only once after an outage and blaming a colleague, so deeper causes remain and the outage recurs.

subtype: Approach: continues asking until a process cause appears and fixes the process [Revision]
passage:
Hi Baljeet,

Thanks for joining the outage review yesterday. Last week we'd said it was one person's slip; this time we went back and asked properly. I've written it up since you're travelling. The site went down after Tuesday's release. Why? A bad setting reached the live site. Why? The deployment doesn't check settings before going out. Why? The check sat on an old list nobody updated. Why? Nobody owned that list after the team changed. Why did it matter? Nothing else would have caught it. We didn't name a person, only a gap. So we've added an automated test that fails the release if a setting is missing, and the list now has an owner each quarter. Could you look over the wording of the test?

Tanuja

qa.q: What did the team add after the review?
qa.a: The team added an automated test that fails the release if a setting is missing.

qa.q: What does Tanuja seem to want from the second review?
qa.a: Tanuja seems committed to fairness and wants the process fixed, not a person blamed, and sounds relieved to have found a real cause.

qa.q: What other step could the team add to prevent similar outages?
qa.a: The team could rehearse a quick rollback of a bad release, since a fast way back limits the damage when a check still misses something.

qa.q: How might Baljeet feel on receiving the write-up?
qa.a: Baljeet probably feels included and trusted, since Tanuja wrote it up for someone travelling and asked for help with the test wording.

grounding: Shows a team revisiting an outage, asking why five times, finding a missing deployment check and adding an automated test instead of assigning blame.

subtype: Approach: shouts out many ideas together before choosing one [Thinking]
passage: In a kindergarten in Singapore, a week before Diwali, the teacher asked, 'How can we decorate our classroom?' Hands shot up and voices tumbled: 'Flowers!' 'Lamps!' 'Paper chains!' 'Rangoli!' Hana shouted, 'Stars!' and Mina yelled, 'Lots of flowers!' The teacher wrote every idea on a big sheet and said no to none. When the shouting stopped, there were nine ideas. Then the teacher said, 'Everyone gets two stickers.' The children stuck them beside their favourites. Paper chains and lamps got the most. Hana clapped. 'Stars can come next time,' said the teacher.

qa.q: How many ideas did the teacher write on the sheet?
qa.a: The teacher wrote nine ideas on the sheet.

qa.q: How did Hana seem to feel when the stickers were counted?
qa.a: Hana seemed happy and fine about it, clapping for paper chains and lamps even though stars did not win.

qa.q: What could the class do so that Hana's idea is not left out?
qa.a: The class could hang a few paper stars on the paper chains, since a small piece of a favourite idea can fit with the chosen ones.

qa.q: How might the teacher have felt while listening to all the shouting?
qa.a: The teacher was probably pleased and amused to see the children so full of ideas, since every idea was written down. 🙂

grounding: Shows children calling out many ideas for festival decorations together, the teacher writing all of them, and the class then voting for two.
